☆ Adaptive Distance Detection and Adaptive Instance Segmentation
Kai Yi Ji
This paper is about object detection model and semantic segmentation model in an FPS game Counter Strike: Condition Zero to detect enemies. Semantic segmentation is pixel-wise detection algorithm. We customized the architecture for semantic segmentation. We used YOLOv5s to train object detection model. After training, the inference time of semantic segmentation was compared to object detection. It was observed that object detection was slightly faster and semantic segmentation is slower but better at detecting the exact shape of the object. However, we found out that this slight difference of inference can grow exponentially if the both models get more complex. To solve this, we propose a novel approach called Adaptive distance detection which combines both algorithms. We will also introduce Adaptive instance segmentation to combine semantic segmentation and panoptic segmentation.

☆ TRACE: Trajectory Synchronization for Training-Free Resolution Extension in Video Generation
Libo Zhu, Fan Li, Zhixin Wang, Binglu Wang, Weisheng Dong, Yulun Zhang
More text-to-video models are available, but many remain limited to low resolutions. Training them for higher resolutions is costly, while existing training-free methods still struggle with fine detail, scene structure, and efficiency. We propose TRACE, a training-free method that synchronizes low- and high-resolution generation trajectories. During early denoising, TRACE aligns predicted scene content at corresponding noise levels. It computes high-resolution updates from low-resolution predictions and the current high-resolution state, without high-resolution model inference. The high-resolution trajectory retains fine-grained variation for generating new details. Local window attention then refines fine details in a shared high-resolution latent state. TRACE checks suspected duplicate subjects against the corresponding low-resolution layout and corrects selected regions and their solver history while preserving detail elsewhere. Experiments across all kinds of video generation backbones and resolutions show improved perceptual quality and text-video alignment over FreeSwim, a state-of-the-art training-free method, with 2.0-2.9x end-to-end speedups. Our code and models will be released at https://github.com/libozhu03/TRACE.
☆ DuoJEPA: Cross-Modal Translation Between Unaligned Self-Supervised Embedding Spaces
Mahmut S. Gokmen, Mitchell A. Klusty, Evan W. Damron, Caroline N. Leach, Samuel E. Armstrong, V. K. Cody Bumgardner
Learning from paired modalities is commonly equated with aligning them: two encoders are trained until the embeddings of a pair coincide in a shared space. We study whether cross-modal retrieval and classification can instead be obtained while the two encoders' own embedding spaces remain directly unaligned. DuoJEPA trains one encoder per modality with the self-supervised LeJEPA objective and appends to each encoder a single transformer layer that translates its embedding into the other encoder's space, supervised by a contrastive objective computed entirely within that target space. No loss term compares the two own spaces directly, although the encoders are optimised jointly through the translation objective. In our experiments, the translator's residual connections determine where the cross-modal pressure is absorbed: with a residual translator the two encoders become directly aligned, whereas with a skipless (residual-free) translator a paired-cosine test detects no alignment in the final models, and at most a weak one in the ablations, at comparable cross-modal performance. The learned class-token translation is well approximated by a single scaled rotation of the source space. We evaluate DuoJEPA on two modality pairs that differ in nearly every respect. On chest radiographs and reports from CheXpert Plus, it attains a zero-shot AUC of 86.6 and a cross-modal retrieval score of 78.5, compared with 60.0 and 64.2 for our reimplementation of LeVLJEPA with the same encoders and data. On Sentinel-2 optical and Sentinel-1 radar imagery, the frozen encoders fall within the range of published Sentinel foundation models under our reproduction of the Copernicus-Bench linear-probe protocol, the translator retrieves the paired image of the other sensor among 4,000 candidates in 77-79% of cases, and a patch-level extension transfers the within-image similarity structure of the scene.
☆ Lang-SVG: Hierarchical Image Vectorization with Language Priors NeurIPS 2026
Xi Liu, Chaoyi Zhou, Run Wang, Jiaang Li, Feng Luo, Junxiang Huang, Siyu Huang
Image vectorization reconstructs raster images as compact scalable vector graph- ics (SVG), providing a structured and editable code representation of images. However, most existing vectorization methods optimize for pixel-level render- ing fidelity, often producing SVGs that lack alignment with human-perceived object-part hierarchies, making them difficult to manipulate. To address this, we propose Lang-SVG, which introduces an explicit tree structure to organize SVG primitives with semantic labels and parent-child relationships. Lang-SVG incorporates granularity-controllable and open-vocabulary segmentation priors to initialize object-part hierarchies and leverages multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with SVG tree context to assign semantic labels to unlabeled nodes. To reduce redundancy, we introduce depth-adaptive simplification to reduce shape complexity and Tree-Guided Pruning and Merging to eliminate redundant SVG nodes. L1-SAM-Prompting further recovers missing regions to improve recon- struction fidelity and structural completeness. Beyond reconstruction fidelity, we introduce a new evaluation protocol that measures structural quality and semantic part alignment. Experiments demonstrate that Lang-SVG achieves state-of-the-art performance in both rendering fidelity and structural quality. Project website: https://xiliu8006.github.io/Lang-SVG/.

♻ ☆ SFL-Net: Dependence-Regularized Latent Pathways for Multi-Contrast MRI-to-tau-PET Synthesis and Component Attribution
Agamdeep S. Chopra, Caitlin Neher, Tianyi Ren, Juampablo E. Heras Rivera, Hesamoddin Jahanian, Mehmet Kurt
Structural MRI-to-tau-PET synthesis estimates molecular imaging patterns from indirect anatomical correlates. We present SFL-Net, a vector-quantized architecture with shared, T1-specific, FLAIR-specific, and joint-input latent pathways. Dependence regularization differentiates these pathways, while latent-derived structural conditioning supports decoding without direct encoder-decoder feature skips. We evaluated SFL-Net and capacity-matched VAE, VQ-VAE, U-Net, and SPADE-U-Net variants using 605 training and 83 internal validation subjects pooled from ADNI-3 and OASIS-3. SFL-Net achieved the lowest raw PET MAE and MSE and the highest PSNR among the implemented models, while SPADE-U-Net variants performed better on several SUVR and staging metrics. Exact coalitional Shapley attribution assigned the largest average marginal contribution to the joint-input pathway, with substantial variation across subjects. These contributions describe decoder dependence under latent replacement and retained structural conditioning; they do not establish identifiable information-theoretic synergy or the incremental benefit of combining MRI contrasts. Predictions showed dynamic-range compression at higher tau burden, and several staging metrics were close to a constant Stage 1 reference. SFL-Net provides a framework for structured latent-component interrogation in multi-input image synthesis, linking architectural pathways to reconstruction behavior.
♻ ☆ Design, Implementation and Evaluation of a Real-Time Remote Photoplethysmography (rPPG) Acquisition System for Non-Invasive Vital Sign Monitoring
Constantino Álvarez Casado, Sasan Sharifipour, Manuel Lage Cañellas, Nhi Nguyen, Le Nguyen, Miguel Bordallo López
The growing integration of smart environments and low-power computing devices, coupled with mass-market sensor technologies, is driving advancements in remote and non-contact-based physiological monitoring. However, deploying these systems in real-time on resource-constrained platforms introduces significant challenges related to scalability, interoperability, and performance. This paper presents a computationally efficient real-time remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) system, designed to extract physiological signals, such as heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation (SpO2), from facial video streams. The system is built on the Face2PPG pipeline, which processes video frames sequentially for rPPG signal extraction and analysis, while leveraging a multithreaded architecture to manage video capture, real-time processing, network communication, and graphical user interface updates concurrently. This design targets continuous operation at 30 frames per second (FPS), with adaptive feedback through a collaborative user interface to guide optimal signal capture conditions. The network interface includes both an HTTP server for continuous video streaming and a RESTful API for on-demand vital sign retrieval. To ensure accurate performance despite limited computational resources, we use a hybrid programming model combining Functional Reactive Programming (FRP) and the Actor Model, allowing event-driven processing and efficient task parallelization. We evaluate HR accuracy on three public datasets (COHFACE, LGI-PPGI, and UBFC-RPPG), and conduct preliminary evaluations of RR on COHFACE and SpO2 on PURE. We also assess the processing time and end-to-end operation of the system on two computers, including live HR and SpO2 agreement with a medical-grade fingertip pulse oximeter across five 10-minute sessions. Our work addresses key challenges in real-time contactless biosignal monitoring.
comment: 33 pages, 4 figures, 11 numbered equations, 6 tables, and 67 references. Evaluated on 4 public datasets and in 5 live 10-minute sessions on 2 computers. Code available at https://github.com/Multimodal-Sensing-Lab/rt-rppg
♻ ☆ Steering Away from Memorization: Reachability-Constrained Reinforcement Learning for Text-to-Image Diffusion
Sathwik Karnik, Juyeop Kim, Sanmi Koyejo, Jong-Seok Lee, Somil Bansal
Text-to-image diffusion models are susceptible to memorization, revealing a fundamental failure to generalize beyond the training set. Current mitigation approaches often sacrifice image quality or prompt alignment to reduce memorization. To address this, we propose Reachability-Aware Diffusion Steering (RADS), an offline-trained, sampling-time control framework that mitigates memorization while maintaining generation fidelity. RADS models the diffusion denoising process as a dynamical system and learns a policy-conditioned reachability value function that estimates future memorization risk along the denoising trajectory. This motivates a constrained reinforcement learning (RL) formulation, where a policy learns to steer the trajectory away from memorization via perturbations in the caption embedding space. Empirical evaluations show that RADS achieves a stronger empirical Pareto frontier between generation diversity (SSCD), quality (FID), and alignment (CLIP) compared to state-of-the-art inference-time baselines. Crucially, RADS applies the learned controller during sampling time, separating memorization mitigation from the pretrained model. Our website is available at: https://s-karnik.github.io/rads-memorization-project-page/.
♻ ☆ ReflFlow: Learning Geometry-Guided Ray Tracing for Dynamic Specular Reconstruction ICML 2026
Jiachen Tao, Junyi Wu, Haoxuan Wang, Zongxin Yang, Dawen Cai, Yan Yan
We present ReflFlow, a novel framework for high-fidelity rendering of dynamic specular scenes by addressing two key challenges: precise reflection direction estimation and physically accurate modeling. To achieve this, we propose a Residual Material-Augmented 2D Gaussian Splatting representation that models dynamic geometry and material properties, allowing accurate reflection ray computation. Furthermore, we introduce a Dynamic Environment Gaussian and a hybrid rendering pipeline that decomposes rendering into diffuse and specular components, enabling physically informed specular synthesis via rasterization and ray tracing. Finally, we devise a coarse-to-fine training strategy to improve optimization stability and promote physically meaningful decomposition. Extensive experiments on dynamic scene benchmarks demonstrate that ReflFlow outperforms prior methods quantitatively and qualitatively, producing sharper and more realistic specular reflections in complex dynamic environments.
comment: ICML 2026. 16 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables, including references and appendices
♻ ☆ DUNE: Disentangling Polysemantic Neurons Without Losing Predictive Performance
Doğukan Bağcı, Bernt Schiele, Simone Schaub-Meyer, Jonas Fischer, Robin Hesse
Deep neural networks (DNNs) are widely used, but understanding what they actually learn remains difficult. A major obstacle is that individual neurons often respond to multiple unrelated concepts, obscuring the network's internal decision process. Existing approaches, such as sparse autoencoders, can disentangle these mixed signals into more meaningful, ``monosemantic'' features, but typically introduce approximation errors that may degrade downstream performance. Consequently, these methods exhibit a Pareto frontier between monosemanticity and functional faithfulness. To address this, we introduce DUNE (disentangling units with no error), a method that decomposes DNN neurons into more monosemantic subunits while preserving their original function by design. DUNE identifies concept-specific contributions from the preceding layer and re-routes them into separate subunits whose aggregation exactly recovers the original activation. DUNE can be applied directly to pretrained models, without labels or training of an auxiliary model. Across several models, including DINOv2, DUNE achieves state-of-the-art or competitive monosemanticity while exactly preserving functional faithfulness, substantially advancing the existing Pareto frontier between these properties. DUNE operates efficiently and enables fine-grained interventions such as concept-specific steering.

♻ ☆ Does Seeing More Mean Knowing More? Mono-Anchored Advantage Normalization for Multi-Source Visual Reasoning NeurIPS 2026
Fanhu Zeng, Zhicong Luo, Zefan Wang, You Li, Chi Chen, Maosong Sun
Visual reasoning through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has achieved remarkable progress. However, when dealing with multi-source inputs, existing approaches tend to treat them as a mere accumulation of information, lacking explicit mechanisms to distinguish whether integrating additional sources yields information gain or introduces interference. Therefore, they struggle to effectively model dynamic interaction when integrating multiple sources, particularly when they differ significantly in physical properties and semantics, e.g., infrared and depth, leading to inferior performance to mono-source reasoning when a certain source holds the dominant signal. To address this issue, we propose MARS, a novel mono-anchored multi-source reasoning framework that models each visual modality as an independent information source. Specifically, by treating mono-source rewards as dynamic anchors, our method explicitly incorporates the information gain introduced by multi-source fusion into advantage normalization and adaptively emphasizes mutual promotion between sources while suppressing potential noise or conflicts during RLVR. From theoretical analysis, our method effectively quantifies information gain introduced by multi-source integration in gradient estimation, enabling consistent modality regulation. Empirical results also show impressive 3.2% and 4.9% performance gains on GRPO and DAPO across diverse datasets, confirming the effectiveness of our method. Code is available at https://github.com/AI9Stars/MARS.
comment: NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ Diffusion Plug-in Priors for Self-Supervised Ultrasound Video Restoration
Chu Chen, Mingduo He, Yining Li, Yinhao Wu, Wei Tang, Yiwen Luo, Yixuan Chen, Pasquale Cascarano, Kangning Cui
Ultrasound videos suffer from hardware-constrained spatial resolution and signal-dependent speckle, while paired low- and high-resolution acquisitions are rarely available. We propose UltraDiff, a self-supervised framework for joint ultrasound video super-resolution and despeckling that uses a frozen pre-trained diffusion model as a plug-in prior. Rather than retraining the model, UltraDiff restores each frame by optimizing the sampler's latent seed under a range-constrained maximum a posteriori-inspired formulation. We derive a speckle-aware data-fidelity term from a Rayleigh scale-family model and characterize its relative-residual and locally variance-adaptive weighting properties. To address degeneracy near zero intensities, we introduce a stabilized surrogate fidelity that is bounded below and strictly convex in log intensity for positive observations in its unclamped form. Total-variation regularization complements the removal of mixed noise, and a temporal seed update warm-starts each frame from the optimized seed of its predecessor, accelerating the convergence. On EchoNet-LVH with simulated speckle and additive noise, UltraDiff with a natural-image prior improves peak signal-to-noise ratio by 1.24\,dB over the strongest baseline, and ultrasound-related priors yield further gains. On 100 real EchoNet-Dynamic videos, UltraDiff reduces the mean absolute error of zero-shot ejection fraction prediction from 7.31 to 6.37 percentage points compared with DUP. These results support ground-truth-free ultrasound video restoration using frozen diffusion priors and a speckle-aware fidelity, without paired training data or model retraining.
♻ ☆ AVI-HT: Adaptive Vision-IMU Fusion for 3D Gloved Hand Tracking NeurIPS 2026
Ziyi Kou, Ankit Kumar, Mia Huang, Taylor Niehues, Vatsal Mehta, Ergys Ristani, Li Guan
We present AVI-HT, an adaptive visual-IMU fusion approach for tracking 3D hand poses by jointly modeling the egocentric images with on-glove 6-DoF IMU signals. AVI-HT significantly improved accuracy and availability, particularly in hand-object interaction (HOI) scenarios involving heavy visual occlusion. Two complementary ingredients underpin its success: (1) synchronized multi-modal training data pairing on-body vision-IMU sensor streams with ground-truth 3D hand poses from a motion-capture system, and (2) a cross-sensor deep attention mechanism that adaptively modulates the trust assigned to the vision and individual IMU sensors. To evaluate AVI-HT in real-world settings, we conduct extensive experiments on our DexGloveHOI dataset that consists of 100K+ pairwise vision-IMU samples with synchronized 3D annotated poses, in which users manipulate a variety of objects during daily tasks. We compare against multiple single- and multi-modal tracking approaches under two hand models (UmeTrack, MANO). The results show that AVI-HT reduces mean keypoint error by 16.1% and its wrist-aligned variant by 24.2% over the baselines. A hand-object contact evaluation shows that AVI-HT keeps finger contacts with the manipulated object more accurately and consistently over time, reducing contact losses by 8.5%. Ablation studies further show that our fusion design outperforms simpler schemes and that the gains grow with occlusion and hold across subjects.

♻ ☆ Anchored Rank-Adversarial Fine-Tuning of Pretrained Visual Place Recognition Models
Mostafa Kira, Bader Rasheed, Manuel Mazzara
Visual place recognition (VPR) localises a camera by retrieving similar geo-tagged images, and current foundation-model VPR models are accurate across cities, seasons and illumination, but not robust to adversarial perturbations: under a white-box attack on the ranking at an imperceptible budget of 1/255, SuperVLAD and BoQ keep at most 0.2% top-1 recall (R@1) on four benchmarks. We propose anchored rank-adversarial fine-tuning (ARAFT), which fine-tunes a released model with a listwise rank loss on each adversarial query's hardest positive and an anchor to the clean descriptor of the frozen pretrained model. Checkpoints are selected under a clean-accuracy budget fixed in advance, and the full trade-off is reported. Within five validation R@1 points of clean cost, plain adversarial training has no admissible checkpoint, whereas ARAFT raises robust R@1 from zero to 47.3 on SuperVLAD and 55.3 on BoQ; plain adversarial training exceeds this only at about three times the clean cost. Against unbudgeted plain adversarial training on the test sets, ARAFT matches its robust R@1 at 2/255 with about ten more clean R@1 points. At 4/255, plain adversarial training is 6-9 robust R@1 points ahead, while ARAFT still keeps its ten-point clean advantage. Developed on SuperVLAD, ARAFT transfers to BoQ without re-tuning, and its robustness holds against stronger optimisers, with no sign of gradient masking.
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables
♻ ☆ GraftRay: Physically Based Mesh Insertion into Gaussian Splatting Scenes via Path Tracing
Jinxin Ai, Matthias Nießner
We present GraftRay, a unified method for physically consistent insertion of mesh objects into 2D and 3D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS/3DGS) indoor scenes. We lift albedo, roughness, metallic and normals from diffusion-based 2D priors onto the Gaussians by back-projection, model windows and lamps as analytic area emitters, and recover their absolute radiance from ordinary LDR captures with a low-dimensional fit over unit-radiance bases. A path tracer over Gaussians and meshes then produces view-consistent shading, interreflections and soft shadows, which are composited onto the original reconstruction by differential rendering, preserving the untouched background. On synthetic, real and generated scenes, GraftRay outperforms recent insertion and inverse-rendering baselines in image fidelity and shadow accuracy at competitive cost, and users prefer its lighting and shadows over those of the baselines.
comment: 8 pages + references, 5 figures, 3 tables
♻ ☆ Addressable Memory for Video World Models
Xindi Wu, Sven Elflein, James Lucas, Olga Russakovsky, Laura Leal-Taixé, Despoina Paschalidou, Jonathan Lorraine, Aljoša Ošep
We study visual persistence in interactive video world models. These models rely on a Key-Value (KV) cache as a growing visual memory to carry forward previously generated frames. However, we find that models can no longer reliably address stored content once rollouts extend beyond the training horizon, because temporal Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) offsets can exceed the training range and the model struggles to retrieve the relevant visual information through attention. Moreover, naively compressing the cache in the RoPE-rotated space degrades memory by averaging keys with incompatible positional phases. To address this, we propose WorldTrace, a training-free memory framework for long-horizon visual persistence. WorldTrace keeps compressed memory addressable by assigning each summary slot a distinct, in-distribution virtual position. Within this cache, WorldTrace uses the model's own attention to decide which observations to retain verbatim and which redundant ones to merge into compressed summaries, all within one bounded addressable memory bank. We evaluate this ability with LoopBench, a benchmark that tests whether a compressed cache can reconstruct a previously visited scene after a long detour. On LoopBench, WorldTrace improves average DINOv2 recall similarity by 32.6% over a sliding window at the same cache budget, extending visually persistent generation without retraining.

Optimization and Control 60
☆ Addendum to "Geodesic fields for Pontryagin type $C^0$-Finsler manifolds"
Hugo Murilo Rodrigues, Ryuichi Fukuoka
In the paper ``Geodesic fields for Pontryagin type $C^0$-Finsler manifolds'', the same authors introduced a geometric object called Pontryagin-type $C^0$-Finsler structures, which includes Finsler structures on a smooth manifold $M$. Such a structure is defined locally by a control system of $C^1$ unit vector fields on an open subset $U$ of $M$, such that Pontryagin's maximum principle (PMP) is applicable. As a result of PMP, we obtain the extended geodesic field $\mathcal{E}$, which is a multivalued vector field on the slit cotangent bundle $T^{\ast}U\backslash 0 = \{(x,α): x\in U, α\in T^{\ast}_x U\}$, such that every minimizing path $x(t)$ on $(U,F)$ is an extremal (projection of a Pontryagin extremal $(x(t),α(t))$). Some time after its introduction, its use and external comments, it is useful to provide remarks that clarify the applicability and limitations of this theory. In addition, we point out two errors contained in that work which, although discernible from the context, we believe should be pointed out. Finally, we prove some cases where the property that a minimizing path is the projection of a Pontryagin extremal can be extended beyond a coordinate system, sometimes to $M$. We also work on the problem of determining when $\mathcal{E}$ does not depend on the control system chosen to represent $F$. In particular, $\mathcal{E}$ satisfies these two properties globally for left-invariant $C^0$-Finsler structures on Lie groups, and for $C^1$-Finsler structures (without the condition of strong convexity).
comment: 9 pages
☆ An Optimized Expansion Auction Integrating Energy, Flexibility, and Network Constraints
Rafael Benchimol Klausner, Alexandre Street, Joaquim Dias Garcia, Luiz Barroso
Auction mechanisms are widely used to support generation investments. In the US, capacity auctions serve as supply-adequacy instruments to address the missing-money problem, whereas in Latin America, energy and capacity auctions procure long-term contracts to support generation expansion. In both settings, accreditation metrics, such as Firm Energy (FE) and Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC), are used to approximate the reliability contribution of selected units and winning projects are selected based on a financial offer. This approach fails to recognize the actual contribution of winners to the multiple services they provide to the system. This limitation becomes more significant with high shares of renewables, as the value of each resource increasingly depends on network and technological constraints, as well as on complementarities within the generation portfolio. Inspired by short-term auctions, such as day-ahead markets, this paper proposes a joint optimization-based auction for generation and transmission investments that internalizes these interactions, capturing the intrinsic value of generation candidates without requiring the computation of FE or ELCC metrics. The auctioneer determines the winning portfolio through an expansion-planning model that explicitly represents network constraints, operational interactions, reliability standards, and multiple scenarios. A case study of the Brazilian system indicates lower system costs, lower risk, and a more diverse portfolio relative to the stylized decoupled procurement approaches currently deployed in many systems.
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
☆ Your PID Is Already a Neural Network: Learning Its Gains with Only Three Weights and No Teacher
Felipe de Jesús Félix-Arredondo, Nezih Nieto-Gutiérrez, Carlos Astengo-Noguez, Alejandro Ucan-Puc
A discrete PID controller is exactly a recurrent neural network, a classical state-space fact: a fixed linear memory of the running integral and the last error, read out by three trainable weights that map one-to-one to the PID gains. Networks with bounded hidden states, such as LSTMs of any width, only approximate it. Trained only on a one-step physical cost (the expected cost of one transition from a fixed state distribution), with no demonstrations, teacher controller, or known gains, the network solves a strongly convex least-squares problem, so gradient descent converges from any initialization to the unique one-step optimal PID gains; the limit network is that PID, with the same action on every error sequence. Partitioned regression then shows what extra capacity buys. Orthogonal residual features keep these gains and improve on the PID if and only if they correlate with the part of the optimal action outside the PID span. On a nonlinear second-order example the gap is 5.88% of the optimal PID cost, and 4.00% against PID with a bias; no controller can improve on PID by more on this objective. A residual started at a tuned PID begins exactly at that PID; at the one-step optimal PID, a fixed-feature residual's first gradient step lowers the cost if and only if its features can improve on the PID. Experiments confirm the realization, recovery, and gap results to numerical precision. On held-out plants of three families, under a protocol frozen before the test data existed, a residual warm-started at a heavily tuned PID and trained with it lowers the long-horizon cost by 3.5%, 3.5%, and 1.9%, with family-wise 95% bounds excluding zero, also under distribution shift; a post hoc comparison with the PID tuned alone suggests that most of it comes from the recurrent part in two families. The primary endpoint, a gain of at least 5% from a generic PID start, is not met in any family.

☆ Fit-LRP: Fitting Linear Relaxations to Polytopes for Neural Network Verification over Non-Convex Regions
Brian Yarbrough, Jesse Wayment, Jingbo Wang, Philip E. Paré, Shreyas Sundaram
State-of-the-art neural network verifiers evaluate linear relaxations over axis-aligned bounding boxes. However, verification domains in cyber-physical systems are rarely boxes. Reachability specifications, obstacle-avoidance constraints, and neural Lyapunov certificates typically yield oblique or non-convex polyhedral regions, over which box-based bounds become extremely loose. This paper proposes Fit-LRP (Fitting Linear Relaxations to Polytopes), a framework the implements exact optimization of affine bounds over non-convex domains (represented by unions of polytopes) by solving a sequence of small, low-dimensional linear programs. Our approach seamlessly enhances the final optimization step of LiRPA and $α,\! β$-CROWN branch-and-bound (BaB) algorithms. In BaB verification, approximating oblique constraints with axis-aligned splits causes severe combinatorial blowup and risks non-termination. By optimizing the final affine bound of a nonlinear function over the exact polyhedral state-space constraints our method eliminates box-induced over-approximations, enabling earlier search-tree pruning. On ARCH-COMP and neural Lyapunov benchmarks, Fit-LRP reduces branching on the hardest region by $47\times$, cuts worst-case verification time by $15\times$, and with region-wise partitioning, verifies on a single CPU $6.1\times$ faster than $α,\! β$-CROWN on a GPU.
☆ Proximal random reshuffling with inexact gradients for nonconvex composite optimization
Boris S. Mordukhovich, Pedro Pérez-Aros
We design and justify a proximal inexact random reshuffling method for minimizing sums of the finite average of functions with Lipschitz continuous gradients and lower semicontinuous regularizers that may be nonconvex. Each epoch visits every component once, using inexact gradients with a prescribed tolerance, and ends with a single proximal step. Our analysis is pathwise: it holds for every sequence of permutations and does not depend on how the reshuffling is performed. We show that when the stepsizes and error tolerances satisfy suitable summability conditions, the objective values converge and every accumulation point is stationary. Furthermore, under the Polyak--Łojasiewicz--Kurdyka condition at a single accumulation point and sufficient decrease of stepsizes, the entire sequence has finite length and converges to that point. For polynomial stepsizes and power-type desingularizing functions, we derive convergence rates for objective values and iterates. Finally, faster objective-value rates are derived when the limit is a local minimizer.

☆ Your Hypergradient is Skewed: Antithetic Neumann Estimation for Bilevel Optimization NeurIPS 2026
Jason Bohne, Pawel Polak, Gary Kazantsev, David Rosenberg
Bilevel optimization is a core tool in practical machine learning workflows, including hyperparameter tuning, data reweighting, robust learning, reinforcement learning, and imbalanced classification. Hypergradient computation requires the inverse of the inner Hessian, typically estimated via a truncated Neumann series. While existing analyses focus on bias and variance, we show that the product structure of the Neumann series introduces a third source of error: skewness. We identify that, unlike ordinary gradients, whose asymmetry is suppressed by mini-batch averaging, the Neumann estimator amplifies skewness across factors, with the third-moment error growing, under weak contraction, with truncation depth, inner condition number, and per-factor noise asymmetry. This arises in many practical settings such as corrupted labels, outliers, heterogeneous or class-imbalanced datasets. To address this, we introduce the Antithetic Neumann Estimator (ANE), which pairs each Hessian sample with a mirrored counterpart around a reference Hessian and averages the resulting inverse-Hessian estimates. With an exact reference, the antithetic product retains only even-order noise, eliminating all odd-order perturbation terms; with an approximate reference, the residual odd-order contribution is bounded linearly in the reference error. ANE requires only a modification of the Hessian vector step and combines with existing stochastic or variance-reduced bilevel methods. We instantiate ANE-SGD and ANE-VR, the latter adding recursive variance reduction. Across robust regression, data cleaning, offline reinforcement learning, and imbalanced classification, ANE-based methods improve on stochastic and variance-reduced baselines on every task (20 seeds each), lowering loss by 4 to 25% relative to the best baseline; the largest gains, on robust regression, are a 25% lower test loss and a 54% higher test r-squared.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
☆ Optimal higher order convergence rates for the MUON optimizer
Thomas Beretti, Thang Do, Steffen Dereich, Arnulf Jentzen
Gradient descent optimization methods are the key tools to train deep neural networks in artificial intelligence systems. In practice, one typically employs suitable accelerated gradient descent optimization methods such as the momentum optimizer, the Adam optimizer, or the MUON optimizer proposed by Jordan et al. in 2024. In 1964 Polyak showed that, in a neighborhood of a local minimizer, the momentum optimizer converges with the rate $(\sqrtχ+1)^{-1}(\sqrtχ-1)$, which is strictly faster than the rate $(χ+1)^{-1}(χ-1)$ of the standard gradient descent optimizer, where $χ\in(1,\infty)$ is the condition number (the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue) of the Hessian of the objective function at the local minimizer. Recently, the same faster rate has been established for the Adam optimizer. In this work we show that the MUON optimizer achieves the same higher speed of convergence and we establish the optimality of the obtained convergence rates. More specifically, we propose a precise concept for measuring the speed of convergence of gradient descent optimization methods, and we establish optimal convergence rates for the standard gradient descent, the momentum, the RMSprop, the Adam, and the MUON optimizers.
comment: 37 pages
☆ Adaptive linear quadratic optimal control for discrete-time stochastic systems
Nian Liu, Cheng Zhao
In this paper, we consider the adaptive linear quadratic optimal control problem for a class of discrete-time stochastic systems, where the system matrix pair $(A,B)$ is unknown and the state weighting matrix $Q$ in the cost function is not necessarily positive semidefinite. Our proposed adaptive optimal control only assumes that the corresponding algebraic Riccati equation has a stabilizing solution, which weakens the standard controllable and observable assumptions used in the literature. To address this problem, we modify a weighted least squares algorithm by incorporating a random regularization method, which ensures the uniform stabilizability of the family of estimated models. Additionally, a diminishing excitation is introduced in the design of the proposed adaptive control to guarantee the strong consistency of the desired components of the estimates. Finally, by leveraging this family of estimates and employing a suitable switching method, we demonstrate that a certainty equivalence control with such a diminishing excitation is an optimal adaptive control.
☆ Sparse PCA with Overlapping Supports: NP-Hardness and an FPTAS
Alberto Del Pia, Dekun Zhou
In sparse principal component analysis (SPCA) with several components, each must be sparse and all must be pairwise orthogonal. When the supports of the components overlap, these two requirements interact. For a covariance matrix of fixed rank, polynomial-time algorithms with optimality or approximation guarantees are known for one component, and for several components with disjoint supports or with a common support. We study the general model, with individual sparsity constants and arbitrary support overlaps. We are given a rational $n\times r$ matrix $R$ and $d$ sparsity constants $s_i \le n$, and the goal is to find an $n\times d$ matrix $X$ with orthonormal columns that maximizes $\|R^\top X\|_F^2$, such that column $i$ has at most $s_i$ non-zero entries. Here $RR^\top$ plays the role of the covariance matrix and has rank at most $r$. We show that SPCA is NP-hard even when $r = d = 2$, but admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) when $r$ and $d$ are fixed. The returned solution has exactly orthonormal columns, and its entries are real algebraic numbers in an exact representation. For fixed $ε$, the number of steps of the algorithm is linear in $n$ up to a polylogarithmic factor. Our approach reduces SPCA to a sparse version of the orthogonal Procrustes problem, that is, to maximizing a linear function over the feasible region of SPCA. We show that this problem is NP-hard even for $d = 2$, and we give an FPTAS for it when $d$ is fixed. This FPTAS combines approximate dynamic programming over the rows, two-column updates that restore exact orthogonality, and an exact computation of the few variables for which these updates are not available.
☆ The One-Skeleton of Multilinear Polytopes and Their Standard Relaxations
Alberto Del Pia, Zihong Xu
Edge-following methods, such as the simplex method, move along edges of a polytope. Their behavior depends on which vertices are adjacent and on the diameter. We study both for the two polytopes of binary polynomial optimization: the multilinear polytope and its standard linear relaxation. For quadratic polynomials, Padberg showed that two integral vertices are adjacent in both polytopes if and only if the variables where they differ induce a connected subgraph. For higher degree, we replace this subgraph by a contracted hypergraph on the same variables, built from the monomials whose constraints tie these variables together. We show that its connectivity decides adjacency in the relaxation but, unlike in the quadratic case, not always in the multilinear polytope. Adjacency is the same in both polytopes exactly when the relaxation has the Trubin property. We investigate when this property holds and characterize it for cubic polynomials. The contracted hypergraph also yields short paths. The diameter of the multilinear polytope is at most the number of variables, and that of the relaxation is linear in the numbers of variables and monomials. Similar linear bounds hold for the number of pivots between bases of the relaxation.
★ Robust Safe Control Under Uncertainty: Estimation, Contraction, and Regret Bounds
Changrui Liu, Liang Wu, Anil Alan, Shengling Shi, Bart De Schutter
Disturbance uncertainty requires safety filters based on control barrier functions (CBFs) to leave a robustness margin, which can alter the nominal control input and degrade closed-loop performance. This paper studies safety and the resulting performance loss for discrete-time nonlinear systems with additive disturbances and polytopic input constraints. We develop a causal disturbance observer and construct two robust barrier conditions. The first uses a time-dependent bound on the estimation error. The second uses a constant margin when the disturbance increments are uniformly bounded and moves the requirement on the initial error from the online filter to an explicit initialization condition. For affine barriers, both filters are quadratic programs. We bound their input deviations from an oracle filter with access to the current disturbance and derive sufficient conditions for uniform contraction of the oracle closed loop. The contraction analysis accounts for state-dependent actuation, unmatched disturbances, and active physical input limits. Combining the sensitivity and contraction estimates gives finite-time dynamic regret bounds that quantify the effects of observer convergence, disturbance variation, and robustness margins. With sublinear cumulative certified disturbance variation and observer innovation error, the bounds yield sublinear regret.

☆ Minimizing Monotone Norms in Fractional Load Balancing
Daniel Blankenburg, Antonia Ellerbrock, Thomas Kesselheim, Jens Vygen
We devise a fully polynomial time approximation scheme for minimizing a monotone norm $\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert$ over a convex set $X\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d_{\geq 0}$. We study the multi-customer setting, where $X=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ and the solution set $X_i\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d_{\geq 0}$ is given by a linear minimization oracle for each customer $i$. Our result is robust in the sense that it allows for approximate linear minimization oracles and approximate KL projections. While such a result (with exact projection) is well-known for the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm via multiplicative weight updates and was recently obtained for ordered norms via a smooth norm approximation and a novel randomization, existing techniques do not extend to general monotone norms. In particular, a key feature used in previous proofs was dual price stability, which was derived from a global contraction property of the KL projection to the dual space $Y$. We show that this property does not extend to general monotone norms. Therefore, we use a different price mechanism, based on the well-known mirror descent paradigm, for which a local contraction property holds and guarantees stability.

The cost of this adjustment is not adequately understood. This paper proposes a method that quantifies, for any approximate solution, the minimum cost of the adjustments that restore AC feasibility, which is a lower bound on the cost of the heuristic adjustments used in practice. We apply it to the DC optimal power flow, the second-order cone and quadratic convex relaxations, and the AC optimal power flow solved to a loose relative tolerance of $10^{-4}$ instead of $10^{-8}$. Relative to the AC optimal power flow solution obtained from a local nonlinear optimization solver, and even with the minimum adjustment, the DC optimal power flow requires adjusting, on average, generators that account for 15.6% of total generation capacity and incurs a 1.10% cost increase; the convex relaxations require more adjustment (17.2% and 16.9%) but smaller cost increases (0.68% and 0.78%); and the loose-tolerance AC optimal power flow requires 6.1% and incurs 0.42%. Finally, we apply the general theory to several specific graph classes and obtain a complete characterization of optimal policies on the one-dimensional lattice, the complete graph and the star graph for every value of the intervention cost.

Moreover, integer variables can destroy attainment only if there are at least two of them and at least one continuous variable. ♻ ☆ Learning to Solve Stochastic Controls with Unknown Drifts and Running Rewards: Theory, Algorithms and Convergence
Jin Ma, Gaozhan Wang, Jianfeng Zhang, Xunyu Zhou
We study continuous-time and possibly high-dimensional stochastic control problems where drift coefficients and running reward functions are unknown. Due to these missing model primitives, we take the exploratory, reinforcement learning (RL) framework of Wang, Zariphopoulou, and Zhou(2020) with relaxed controls and entropy regularization. The objective is to develop theoretically grounded, efficient and scalable RL algorithms to learn both the optimal value functions (which also solve the exploratory HJB equation) and optimal exploratory feedback control policies. When the diffusion coefficients do not contain control, we employ probabilistic representations of both the optimal value function and its gradient based on an auxiliary state process depending only on the diffusion part of the original dynamics. With a delicate analysis on some properly defined mappings and their fixed points, this leads to the introduction of our policy iteration algorithms and their convergence. We demonstrate the performance of our algorithms through various numerical examples. Finally, we study a special control-dependent diffusion case where probability representation of the Hessian is called for.

♻ ☆ Discrete Model-Based Diffusion for Combinatorial Optimization in Multi-Robot Task Allocation
Haejoon Lee, Thomas Marshall Vielmetti, Xinyi Wang, Dimitra Panagou
Decision making in multi-robot systems often involves discrete decision variables, leading to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems that must be solved within seconds for near real-time implementation. Denoising diffusion has emerged as a powerful tool for such problems, but existing approaches face a trade-off: Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) incorporates diffusion in sampling-based optimization (SBO) without training but only over continuous spaces, while existing diffusion-based combinatorial solvers operate over discrete spaces but require offline training. To this end, we propose Discrete Model-Based Diffusion (Discrete MBD), a training-free SBO method that directly optimizes discrete variables by approximating categorical reverse transition distributions through Monte Carlo sampling. We establish a finite-step lower bound on the probability of finding a global minimizer and show that this bound converges to one as the number of denoising steps increases. Extensive experiments on generic integer programs and heterogeneous multi-robot coalition formation and scheduling demonstrate that Discrete MBD outperforms SBO baselines in nearly all settings while achieving solution quality competitive with that of mixed-integer programming and reinforcement learning methods at a fraction of their computational cost.

♻ ☆ Learning-enabled Acceleration of Scenario-based Model Predictive Control
Trinh Tran, Binh Nguyen, Truong X. Nghiem
Scenario-based model predictive control (SBMPC) is a variant of model predictive control (MPC) that explicitly accounts for uncertainty by optimizing control actions over multiple predicted scenarios. However, its computational complexity increases rapidly with the number of scenarios and prediction horizon, limiting its applicability to real-time planning and control. This paper presents a learning-accelerated Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm for efficiently solving SBMPC problems by leveraging parallel computing and Moreau envelope learning, while maintaining high solution accuracy. We reformulate the SBMPC problems into consensus forms that can be decomposed via ADMM, separating the scenario-dependent dynamics from non-anticipativity constraints and enabling parallel updates across scenarios and time steps. Building on this decomposition, we utilize a learning-to-optimize scheme that leverages Moreau envelope learning of the cost function to accelerate the primal update in ADMM, thereby reducing computation time. The proposed framework is evaluated on a microgrid energy management problem subject to load and renewable generation uncertainties. Comparisons with IPOPT and MadNLP, two popular and modern nonlinear programming solvers, demonstrate substantial computational speedups while maintaining reliable closed-loop control performance.
♻ ☆ Linearize or Discretize First? Error Estimates under Mesh-Uniform Regularity and Exponential Stability for the KdV Equation with Boundary Dissipation
Kangsheng Liu
We study the Korteweg-de Vries equation on a bounded interval with boundary dissipation, and its spatial semidiscretization by a weighted cubic Hermite Galerkin method. A small nonlinear wave can be approximated by a linear discrete simulation in two orders: linearize first and then discretize, or discretize first and then linearize. Both orders lead to the same total error. They divide this error differently between linearization and discretization. The difference of the two divisions is what we call the ordering error. We show that it is quadratic in the size of the initial datum and carries a positive power of the mesh size, for all time. It can be used to assess the effect of a coarse-mesh correction for nonlinear problems. For the continuous problem, the solution map is analytic, and the semigroup of the linearized equation has Crandall-Pazy regularity with the exact index 3/2. For the weighted scheme, the discrete semigroups of the linearized equation inherit exponential stability, Kato smoothing and Crandall-Pazy regularity, with bounds uniform in the mesh size. The nonlinear solution maps are analytic, also uniformly in the mesh size. These properties give error estimates in which the error and the datum are measured in the same norm: in the energy norm, in $H_0^1$ and in $H^2$. On every interval $[t_0,\infty)$, $t_0>0$, same-norm convergence holds uniformly on balls at algebraic rates. The ordering error is of order $h^{1/6}$ times the square of the energy norm of the datum, uniformly for all $t\ge0$.

♻ ☆ A Sequential Cubic Programming Method with Second-Order Complexity Guarantees for Equality Constrained Optimization
Nikos Dimou, Michael J. O'Neill
We develop a new method for equality constrained optimization problems based on a sequential cubic programming framework. Each iteration utilizes a step decomposition based on the Jacobian of the constraints into a normal and a tangential component, the latter of which is found by solving a subproblem involving cubic regularization. The method incorporates second-order correction steps as necessary to ensure global convergence to second-order stationary points as well as local quadratic convergence. In addition, we show that the algorithm is the first to obtain worst case complexity guarantees on the order of $\mathcal{O}(ε_g^{-3/2})$ for the gradient of the Lagrangian, $\mathcal{O}(ε_H^{-3})$ in terms of second-order stationarity, and $\mathcal{O}(ε_c^{-1})$ in terms of the constraint violation. These are the best known complexity guarantees of any method for this class of problems.

Using point process theory, we are able to describe the locations of zeroes or maxima, their number, as well as their distribution over a given window of observation. ♻ ☆ Dynamic Programming for A Linear-Gaussian Dual Control Problem
Ying Wang, Yuchao Li, Håkan Hjalmarsson
We consider an infinite-horizon discounted dynamic programming (DP) problem for a countable-innovation belief-state model. The model is a surrogate for a linear-Gaussian dual control problem involving an unknown parameter vector and Gaussian observation noise. The surrogate preserves the first two moments of the Gaussian innovation and the resulting posterior second-moment structure. We allow unbounded belief and control spaces and nonnegative stage costs with quadratic growth in the posterior mean and covariance. Using a posterior-moment weight, we show that the Bellman operator is a contraction in a weighted sup-norm space. We characterize the optimal cost as the unique solution of the Bellman equation in this space, establish the existence of optimal stationary policies. We further prove weighted sup-norm convergence of value iteration, policy iteration, and optimistic policy iteration under vanishing approximation errors. The convergence results under vanishing approximation errors rely on general weighted sup-norm contraction properties and are applicable beyond the particular dual control problem considered here.
♻ ☆ A Generalization of the Passivity Theorem and the Small Gain Theorem Based on $ρ$-Stability, with Application to a Parameter Adaptation Algorithm for Recursive Identification

The usual passivity theorem considers a closed-loop, the direct chain of which consists of a strictly passive stable operator $H_{1}$, and the feedback chain of which consists of a passive operator $H_{2}$. Then the closed-loop is stable. Let $ρ>1$. We show here that the closed-loop is still stable when the direct chain consists of a strictly $ρ^{-1}$-passive $% ρ^{-1}$-stable operator (a weaker condition than above) and the feedback chain consists of a $ρ$-passive operator (a stronger condition than above). Variations on the theme of the small gain theorem (incremental or not) can be made similarly. This approach explains the results obtained in a paper on identification which was recently published.

♻ ☆ Duality for the Adversarial Total Variation
Leon Bungert, Lucas Schmitt
Adversarial training of binary classifiers can be reformulated as regularized risk minimization involving a nonlocal total variation. Building on this perspective, we establish a characterization of the subdifferential of this total variation using duality techniques. To achieve this, we derive a dual representation of the nonlocal total variation and a related integration-by-parts formula, involving a nonlocal gradient and divergence. We provide such duality statements both in the space of continuous functions vanishing at infinity on proper metric spaces and for the space of essentially bounded functions on separable metric spaces. Furthermore, under some additional conditions we provide characterizations of the subdifferential in these settings.

♻ ☆ Precise Convergence Speed of Clipped SGD
David A. R. Robin
We present a tightened convergence analysis of clipped gradient descent on $(L_0, L_1)$-smooth functions, with quantitative constants. Building on the ideas of Koloskova et al (2023), we refactor several case disjunctions to reveal the central role of a control of the bias derived from fundamental properties of $\ell_2$-projection, simplifying proofs. We also extend the domain of validity from $η\leq 1 / (9 β)$ to $η< 1 /β$ where $β= L_0 + c L_1$ for clipping constant $c$, which matches the more traditional analysis of smooth functions. We strengthen the convergence criterion from $\left( \min_{t < T} \mathbb{E}[\lVert \nabla f(x_t) \rVert_2] \right)$ to $\left( \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t < T} \mathbb{E}[\lVert \nabla f(x_t) \rVert_2] \right)$ with matching speed, and lower the final achievable floor from $\mathcal{O}(\min(σ^2/c, σ))$ to the more precise $6 \min(σ^2 /c, 3 σ)$.

♻ ☆ An efficient mixed-integer linear programming formulation for solving influence diagrams
Topias Terho, Fabricio Oliveira, Ahti Salo, Pedro Munari
Influence diagrams represent decision-making problems with interdependencies between random events, decisions, and consequences. Traditionally, they have been solved using tailored algorithms that determine the expected utility-maximizing decision strategy. Towards this end, most recent state-of-the-art solution approaches convert them into mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) models that can be solved using off-the-shelf MILP solvers. Computationally, these approaches are most efficient for influence diagrams that represent periodic (or sequential) decision processes, which can be cast as partially observable Markov Decision Processes. However, they are inefficient for problems that lack this periodic structure or whose influence diagrams have large state spaces. The efficient MILP formulation presented in this paper is specifically designed for influence diagrams that are challenging for earlier MILP formulations. Additionally, this formulation can be adapted to optimize conditional value-at-risk and to incorporate chance and logical constraints, thereby retaining the modeling flexibility of MILP-based methods. Finally, computational experiments on a range of problems from the literature are reported to show that the proposed formulation is much more efficient than earlier MILP formulations, particularly in problems which cannot be modeled as partially observable Markov decision processes and which lead to influence diagrams whose decision or chance nodes may have large state spaces.
♻ ☆ Wolfe's Minimum-Norm-Point Method Generalizes the Simplex Method
Yann Disser, Nils Mosis
Wolfe's method computes the point of minimum Euclidean norm in the convex hull of finitely many points. The method is parameterized by an insertion rule and it has been an open problem whether Wolfe's original rule guarantees a polynomial number of iterations (De Loera, Haddock, and Rademacher; STOC'18). We resolve this question by proving an exponential lower bound. In fact, we establish a tight connection to the simplex method for linear programming that allows us to transfer many lower bounds for simplex pivot rules to corresponding insertion rules of Wolfe's method. These include not only Wolfe's linopt rule via Dantzig's pivot rule, but also many other classical, randomized and history-based rules. As a corollary, we obtain the first exponential example for the Lawson-Hanson algorithm for nonnegative least squares, as well as PSPACE-hardness of deciding whether the linopt rule ever uses a given point.

♻ ☆ ReLU Networks for Model Predictive Control: Network Complexity and Performance Guarantees
Xingchen Li, Keyou You
Recent years have witnessed a resurgence in using ReLU neural networks (NNs) to represent model predictive control (MPC) policies. However, determining the sufficient network complexity to ensure closed-loop guarantees remains a fundamental open problem. This involves a critical precision-complexity trade-off: undersized networks may fail to capture the MPC policy, while oversized ones may outweigh the benefits of ReLU network approximation. In this work, we project the MPC actions onto a tightened constraint set to satisfy the hard constraints, and establish a state-dependent Lipschitz continuity property for the optimal MPC cost function, which enables sharp convergence analysis of the closed-loop system. For the first time, we derive explicit bounds on ReLU network width and depth for approximating MPC policies with closed-loop guarantees. To reduce network complexity for the convergence to user-specified target sets, we propose a non-uniform error framework with a state-aware scaling function to adaptively adjust both the input and output of the ReLU network. Our contributions provide a foundational step toward certifiable ReLU NN-based MPC.
♻ ☆ Dual-Inertial Bregman Methods with Energy-Based Safeguarding
Kangming Chen
We study dual-inertial (DI) Bregman proximal methods for convex optimization via an exact representation of the signed energy drift between dual-coordinate and primal affine interpolation. For unrestarted DI, bounded one-sided directional curvature gives a last-iterate objective-gap rate $\mathcal{O}((1+\log N)/N^2)$ after $N$ iterations, which improves to $\mathcal{O}(N^{-2})$ under weighted summability. The energy balance also provides a computable acceptance test, which we use in two safeguards. The restart safeguard attains a global $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$ rate after $T$ proximal calls, including rejected trials. Under local quadratic growth and kernel regularity, it restarts only finitely often and eventually converges linearly. The non-restarting safeguard preserves the quadratic weight recurrence via dual substeps. Every fallback terminates without triangle scaling, yielding a $\mathcal{O}(N^{-2})$ rate in outer iterations and an $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$ rate in calls, which improves to $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$ when the cumulative fallback cost is $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Experiments on relative-entropy regression and nonnegative least squares illustrate the results.
♻ ☆ $γ$-weakly $θ$-up-concavity: A Unified Framework for Non-Convex Optimization Beyond DR-Submodular and OSS Functions
Mohammad Pedramfar, Vaneet Aggarwal
Many objectives in machine learning and combinatorial optimization are non-concave. We introduce $γ$-weak $θ$-up-concavity, a first-order condition for nonnegative monotone functions in which a scaling function $θ$ lets the curvature change with the size of the solution. The resulting class strictly contains monotone DR-submodular functions and One-Sided Smooth (OSS) functions. It also contains functions whose marginal gains first increase and then decrease, and functions that vanish faster than any power of the norm at the origin. We construct a surrogate gradient from gradients along the segment from the origin to the current point and prove an upper-linearization inequality with a point-dependent approximation coefficient. Restricting actions to the closed convex hull of the coordinate-wise maximal feasible points makes this coefficient uniformly positive, with a value determined by the curvature parameters and the geometry of the feasible set. Standard reductions to linear optimization then give offline approximation algorithms and online algorithms with regret guarantees. The coefficient matches the optimal one for DR-submodular maximization and improves the best known coefficients for OSS maximization over matroid constraints whenever the OSS parameter is positive.

♻ ☆ Regularization and Full Support for the CBO Equation with Measure Initial Data
Lukang Sun
We prove global well-posedness and regularization for the isotropic consensus-based optimization equation with initial probability measures of finite fourth moment. Under suitable weight decay assumptions, after any nonconstant consensus motion, both the density and the consensus trajectory become smooth, and all spatial Sobolev norms are locally bounded in time. The proof uses a Fourier commutator estimate, localization and iteration, followed by a nonlinear time bootstrap. Counterexamples show that smoothing can fail at a stationary consensus point. For non-Dirac initial data, we also prove positivity away from the consensus point and full support at every positive time in all dimensions.

♻ ☆ Strategically Robust Linear Quadratic Dynamic Games
Boris Velasevic, Nicolas Lanzetti, Eric Mazumdar
We study linear quadratic dynamic games where players are uncertain about each other's control policies or goals and consequently seek to be strategically robust. Building on recent work on strategically robust and risk-averse game theory, we first formalize the problem of strategically robust linear quadratic dynamic games. We show that these can be rewritten as simple transformations of linear quadratic games in which each player chooses a controller in a fictitious game in which they are faced with an adversary who is penalized for deviating from the other players' policies. This formulation naturally induces a novel notion of dynamic equilibrium, which we call a strategically robust dynamic equilibrium. We establish existence and uniqueness (in the subgame-perfect sense) of such equilibria and show that the equilibrium policies are Markovian, linear, and can be efficiently computed via coupled backward Riccati equations. Through numerical simulations, including experiments in a network game, we illustrate the benefits of strategic robustness in designing robust and resilient decentralized control schemes. Our experiments also expose a "free-lunch" phenomenon in games in which robustness does not incur a corresponding loss in performance but can yield improvements in players' utilities and social welfare.

♻ ☆ Time-optimal problem in the space of probability measures
Yurii Averboukh, Ekaterina Kolpakova
This paper focuses on the value function in the time-optimal problem for a continuity equation in the space of probability measures. We derive the dynamic programming principle for this problem. Using this principle, we prove that the Kruzhkov transform of the value function is a unique discontinuous viscosity solution to the corresponding Dirichlet problem for the Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Finally, we establish the $Γ$-convergence of the value function in a perturbed problem to the value function in the unperturbed problem.

♻ ☆ Efficient Alternating Minimization with Applications to Weighted Low Rank Approximation ICLR 2025
Zhao Song, Mingquan Ye, Junze Yin, Lichen Zhang
Weighted low rank approximation is a fundamental problem in numerical linear algebra, and it has many applications in machine learning. Given a matrix $M \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, a non-negative weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n \times n}$, a parameter $k$, the goal is to output two matrices $X,Y\in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$ such that $\| W \circ (M - X Y^\top) \|_F$ is minimized, where $\circ$ denotes the Hadamard product. It naturally generalizes the well-studied low rank matrix completion problem. Such a problem is known to be NP-hard and even hard to approximate assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis [GG11, RSW16]. Meanwhile, alternating minimization is a good heuristic solution for weighted low rank approximation. In particular, [LLR16] shows that, under mild assumptions, alternating minimization does provide provable guarantees. In this work, we develop an efficient and robust framework for alternating minimization that allows the alternating updates to be computed approximately. For weighted low rank approximation, this improves the cost of each iteration of [LLR16] from $\|W\|_0k^2$ to $\|W\|_0 k$ where $\|W\|_0$ denotes the number of nonzero entries of the weight matrix. At the heart of our framework is a high-accuracy multiple response regression solver together with a robust analysis of alternating minimization. We also replace the random initialization of [LLR16], whose claimed guarantee fails, by subspace iteration from a Gaussian start, so our total running time of $\widetilde O((\|W\|_0 k+nk^3)\log(1/ε))$ includes the initialization. In exchange, our guarantee needs the weight matrix to be within spectral distance $γn$ of the all-ones matrix for a $γ$ that is polynomially small in $n$.
comment: ICLR 2025. This version replaces the random initialization, whose claimed guarantee fails, by subspace iteration, and states the main theorem with all the conditions it needs, including a stronger closeness condition on the weights. The running time bound is unchanged
♻ ☆ Low Rank Matrix Completion via Robust Alternating Minimization in Nearly Linear Time ICLR 2024
Yuzhou Gu, Zhao Song, Junze Yin, Lichen Zhang
Given a matrix $M\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, the low rank matrix completion problem asks us to find a rank-$k$ approximation of $M$ as $UV^\top$ for $U\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times k}$ and $V\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ by only observing a few entries specified by a set of entries $Ω\subseteq [m]\times [n]$. In particular, we examine an approach that is widely used in practice -- the alternating minimization framework. Jain, Netrapalli, and Sanghavi [JNS13] showed that if $M$ has incoherent rows and columns, then alternating minimization provably recovers the matrix $M$ by observing a nearly linear in $n$ number of entries. While the sample complexity has been subsequently improved [GLZ17], alternating minimization steps are required to be computed exactly. This hinders the development of more efficient algorithms and fails to depict the practical implementation of alternating minimization, where the updates are usually performed approximately in favor of efficiency. In this paper, we take a major step towards a more efficient and error-robust alternating minimization framework. To this end, we develop an analytical framework for alternating minimization that can tolerate a moderate amount of errors caused by approximate updates. Moreover, our algorithm runs in time $\widetilde O(|Ω| k)$, which is nearly linear in the time to verify the solution while preserving the sample complexity. This improves upon all prior known alternating minimization approaches which require $\widetilde O(|Ω| k^2)$ time.

♻ ☆ Local Linear Convergence of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers for Semidefinite Programming under Strict Complementarity
Shucheng Kang, Xin Jiang, Heng Yang
We investigate the local linear convergence properties of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) when applied to Semidefinite Programming (SDP). A longstanding belief suggests that ADMM is only capable of solving SDPs to moderate accuracy, primarily due to its sublinear worst-case complexity and empirical observations of slow convergence. We challenge this notion by introducing a new sufficient condition for local linear convergence: as long as the converged primal-dual optimal solutions satisfy strict complementarity, ADMM attains local linear convergence, independent of nondegeneracy conditions. Our proof is based on a direct local linearization of the ADMM operator and a refined error bound for the projection onto the positive semidefinite cone, improving previous bounds and revealing the anisotropic nature of projection residuals. Extensive numerical experiments confirm the significance of our theoretical results, demonstrating that ADMM achieves local linear convergence and computes high-accuracy solutions in a variety of SDP instances, including those cases where nondegeneracy fails. Furthermore, we identify where ADMM struggles, linking these difficulties with near violations of strict complementarity-a phenomenon that parallels recent findings in linear programming.
♻ ☆ Nonlinear Eigen-approach ADMM for Sparse Optimization on Stiefel Manifold
Jiawei Wang, Li Wang, Richard Yi Da Xu, Ren-Cang Li
With growing interest in machine learning and data science, creating efficient algorithms to optimize various dimension reduction objectives has become particularly important. This paper is concerned with optimization problems on the Stiefel manifold whose objective functions take the form as the sum of a smooth function and a nonsmooth one. A common practice is to split such a problem into a smooth optimization subproblem on the Stiefel manifold and a nonsmooth one and solve them by some version of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Usually the smooth subproblem is solved by standard optimization techniques skillfully adapting to the manifold. However, often the smooth subproblem has strong linear algebra characteristics which, if carefully exploited, can lead to much more efficient solvers than the standard optimization techniques that ignore the characteristics. In this paper, it is proposed to tackle the smooth subproblem through a nonlinear eigen-approach which can fully utilize rich linear algebra structures that dominantly present in objective functions from today's data science applications. We conduct convergence analysis and analyze computational complexity for obtaining an $ε$-stationary point. Numerical experiments demonstrate the advantages of the proposed algorithm compared to the state-of-the-art approaches.

☆ Two-Stage Mixed-Integer Quadratic Programming in Polynomial Time
Alberto Del Pia
Lenstra showed that mixed-integer linear programming can be solved in polynomial time when the number of integer variables is fixed and the number of continuous variables is arbitrary. Mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) can be solved in polynomial time when the total number of variables is fixed. However, since MIQP is NP-hard already without integer variables, the analog of Lenstra's result fails unless P = NP. Hence, polynomial-time algorithms for MIQP with an arbitrary number of continuous variables must exploit additional structure. We study MIQPs with two-stage structure, which underlies Benders decomposition and two-stage stochastic programming. A few linking variables, including all integer variables, are coupled with many blocks of continuous variables that interact only through them, both in the constraints and in the objective. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for MIQP with an arbitrary quadratic objective when the number of linking variables and the block size are fixed, while the number of blocks, and hence the number of variables, is arbitrary. The case with no blocks is MIQP in fixed dimension. None of our assumptions can be dropped. Unless P = NP, the number of linking variables and the block size must both be fixed, the blocks cannot interact or contain integer variables, and large blocks cannot be allowed even if their objective is linear. Unless FPT = W[1], the exponent of the running time must depend on both the number of linking variables and the block size.
☆ A family of alternating projection examples whose Cesàro means fail to converge strongly
Heinz H. Bauschke, Tran Thanh Tung
In 1965, Bregman proved that the sequence of iterates of the method of alternating projections applied to two closed convex sets with nonempty intersection in a Hilbert space converges weakly to a point in the intersection. The question whether this convergence may actually fail to be strong was settled in a seminal paper by Hundal in 2004. He provided a counterexample featuring a halfspace and a closed convex cone generated by a certain curve. While largely elementary, the details of Hundal's construction and analysis are quite involved. We revisit this seminal example and present a family of such examples that allows for simpler proofs. Our generating curve combines unit vectors with Gaussian inner products and a height determined by a scalar function. The orbits converge weakly --- but not strongly --- to the origin, while their norms have a positive limit for which we give explicit lower bounds. We also prove that the associated Cesàro means behave likewise; in fact, this is generalized to alternating proximal mappings whose composition has a fixed point. Finally, these orbits allow interpretations in the context of projected-gradient, proximal-point, and gradient-descent algorithms.
☆ Improved last-iterate bounds for SGD with and without replacement
Yimin Zhong, Jiaxin Zhou
In this work, we study last-iterate convergence bounds for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on convex and $β$-smooth loss functions and improve the bound from $\cO((\log T)^3/T)$ to $\cO((\log T)^3/(T\log\log T))$ in the interpolation regime. The improvement comes from applying a horizon-dependent multiscale estimate of gradients to the comparison of trajectories. The bound applies to both sampling with replacement and sampling without replacement within one pass.
☆ Distributionally Robust BEST-RQ For Speech Representation Learning
Muhammad Khan, Xiaodong Cui, Brian Kingsbury, George Saon
BEST-RQ, based on random projection and quantization, has been a well-established self-supervised learning approach to learn speech representations from large-scale unlabeled audio due to its high performance and efficiency. However, in BEST-RQ representations learned by random quantization can be sensitive to the choice of quantization targets. To address this issue, we propose a distributionally robust extension of BEST-RQ that seeks representations robust across multiple quantization configurations. Specifically, we define groups by codebooks and formulate the training as a group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problem. Rather than optimizing solely for the average loss across groups, our approach adaptively reweights groups to emphasize those performing poorly. Additionally, we regularize DRO with a Kullback-Leibler divergence to prevent excessive distribution deviation. We evaluate our approach on the Multilingual LibriSpeech dataset and show that the distributionally robust BEST-RQ achieves superior performance over the conventional uniform average across multiple codebooks.
☆ Compactness-uniqueness method for null controllability
Guillaume Olive
We develop the compactness--uniqueness method for the null controllability of abstract linear control systems on Banach spaces. Our first main result characterizes the null controllable states for systems that are null controllable up to finite dimensional spaces, and shows that null controllability is then equivalent to the Fattorini--Hautus test. Our second main result gives a dual counterpart of this assumption, an observability inequality with a suitable compact remainder. These results unify and extend several known results, such as those on heat equations with nonlocal terms and on the simultaneous controllability of systems. Finally, for a transport equation with nonlocal terms from population dynamics, we characterize the null controllable states after a sharp time, including in the non-reflexive space $L^1$.
☆ Stability of equilibria in discrete-time modified-gradient systems and the multivariate breeder's equation
Benjamin J. Ridenhour
The multivariate breeder's equation $Δ\bar z=G\nabla\ln\bar W$ is a widely used discrete-time modified-gradient system describing the evolution of continuous traits in organisms. This system could more conventionally be expressed as $x_{k+1}=x_k+P_k\nabla f(x_k)$. For its continuous-time counterpart $x'=P(t)\nabla f(x)$, it has been proven that an isolated local maximum of $f$ is uniformly stable whenever $P(t)$ is positive semidefinite, as is the case for the "$G$-matrix." Furthermore, the continuous time system is uniformly asymptotically stable when the maximum is an isolated critical point and $\int_0^\inftyλ_1(P(t))\,dt=\infty$. We show that the literal discrete analog of this result is false: with constant positive definite $P$ the iterates can oscillate or diverge. The result is restored by a single additional hypothesis, a uniform bound on the largest eigenvalue of $P_k$, $λ_n$, such that $λ_n(P_k)\le 2/L$ where $L$ is a local Lipschitz constant of $\nabla f$. Under this bound the maximum is uniformly stable; under a stricter version together with $\sum_kλ_1(P_k)=\infty$, the maximum is uniformly asymptotically stable. Given these hypotheses, a level-set estimate of the basin of attraction carries over. Both bounds are sharp, and each remaining hypothesis is shown to be necessary. Biologically, the bound says that genetic variance in every direction must be small relative to the curvature of log mean fitness; outside this regime the mean phenotype can overshoot a fitness peak as hypothesized by Fisher's geometric model. As further application of our results, the same conditions apply to the mean update of Gaussian evolutionary optimization algorithms, in which the covariance of the search population plays the role of $G$.

Depth-first B&B uses less memory and can find feasible solutions even when the search does not finish within the time limit. Further progress is constrained by weak physical-financial loss validation, incomplete representation of systemic and evolving portfolio risk, and limited empirical and actuarial grounding of insurance-decision feedback. Research priorities include stronger physical-financial data linkage, forward-looking portfolio assessment, multi-timescale decision feedback, and empirical validation. Addressing these priorities would help move power-system insurance from fragmented applications toward a more coherent approach to residual-risk management in future power systems.
