The unavailable tensors $\nabla^{p-1}f$ and $\nabla^pf$ are reconstructed from central finite differences of $\nabla^{p-2}f$. Since the two reconstructions have different point-query costs, we use a block length $m$ for the order-$p$ approximation and a subblock length $\ell\leq m$ for the order-$(p-1)$ approximation. The latter is transported between consecutive reconstruction points using the stored order-$p$ approximation. This leads to an adaptive regularization method that does not require prior knowledge of the Lipschitz constant. We prove finite termination at an $ε$-approximate first-order stationary point and derive an explicit bound on the number of bundled order-$(p-2)$ oracle queries. For $m=(p-2)n^2$ and $\ell=(p-2)n$, the accuracy-dependent term has dimension--accuracy scaling $n^{3/p}ε^{-(p+1)/p}$. Thus the method retains the $ε^{-(p+1)/p}$ dependence of full order-$p$ regularization while using derivatives only through order $p-2$. Within the dense reconstruction framework considered here, using separate block and subblock lengths gives dimension dependence of order $n^{3/p}$, compared with $n^{4/p}$ when a common length is imposed.

Without assuming strong convexity, we establish global well-posedness and simultaneous $\mathcal O(t^{-2})$ decay rates for the constraint violation and the objective residual when $α\geq3$ and the extrapolation parameter satisfies a suitable compatibility condition. Under stricter parameter conditions, with $α>3$, we further prove that the primal-dual trajectory converges to a Karush--Kuhn--Tucker pair, both residuals decay as $o(t^{-2})$. We combine ideas from hybrid systems theory and infinite-dimensional systems to produce operator-based stability conditions, which can be analytically or numerically checked via convex programming. As an application, linear switched systems are shown to be an exact special case: reformulated as impulsive systems with unit-norm selector jumps, they inherit non-coercive and clock-dependent dwell-time stability conditions on both Banach and Hilbert spaces. ♻ ☆ Convergence Analysis of an Upwind Finite-Difference Scheme for Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equations
Daisuke Inoue, Nao Hamamuki, Yuji Ito, Takahito Kashiwabara, Norikazu Saito, Hiroaki Yoshida
We study the convergence of an upwind finite-difference scheme for Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations on a one-dimensional periodic domain, considering both the value function and the feedback control selected by the discrete pointwise minimization. For classical value functions whose time and spatial derivatives are Hölder continuous in their respective variables, we bound the error at the grid points by a constant times the sum of the time step and spatial mesh width each raised to their common Hölder exponent. This yields first-order convergence when these derivatives are Lipschitz continuous and the meshes are refined proportionally. Under additional spatial regularity of the problem data, we also prove convergence of both one-sided difference quotients of the discrete value function to the spatial derivative of the value function: the integral over space and time of the absolute error tends to zero for each difference quotient. We further establish convergence of the discrete controls to the continuous feedback control when the continuous pointwise minimizer is unique, regardless of how the discrete minimizers are selected. These theoretical results are supported by numerical experiments that illustrate the accuracy of the value-function approximation and the behavior of the computed feedback controls.

Ala' Alalabi, Lorena Bociu, Paul Manns
We study coefficient identification problems for elliptic partial differential equations with total variation regularization and control constraints. Existing related literature relies on continuity and differentiability properties of the control-to-state operator with respect to the $L^\infty$-norm. While this is sufficient for deriving optimality conditions, it is not well-suited for numerical algorithms, as it neglects the spatial extent of perturbations and leads to a qualitative discrepancy compared to $L^q$-norms with $q < \infty$. In this work, we address this gap by exploiting $W^{1,s}$-regularity results to establish differentiability properties of the control-to-state operator with respect to $L^q$-norms for finite $q$. Based on this framework, we derive first- and second-order differentiability results for the reduced objective functional and establish first-order optimality conditions involving a restricted subdifferential characterization of the total variation seminorm and corresponding regularity of the associated multipliers. Building on this, we analyze a nonsmooth trust-region method based on an $L^r$-trust region for $r > 0.5 q$ and prove its convergence to first-order stationary points.
♻ ☆ Abs-Smooth Frank-Wolfe Method: Primal-Dual Analysis, Heavy Ball Momentum, and Inexact Oracles

We study projection-free optimization for convex objectives that satisfy abs-smoothness, a structural property that captures many non-smooth yet piecewise smooth functions arising, e.g., in modern machine learning models. We develop a unified framework for Abs-Smooth Frank-Wolfe methods, establishing a clean primal-dual analysis that guarantees convergence without requiring classical smoothness assumptions. Our framework extends the available results in two important directions. First, we introduce a heavy ball momentum variant and show that momentum can be incorporated naturally under abs-smoothness while preserving convergence guarantees. Second, we analyze inexact minimization oracles, demonstrating robustness to approximate inner solutions. Moreover, we relax the full convexity assumption and study the case where convexity holds only for the piecewise linear approximations of the objective, further broadening the applicability of conditional gradient methods to a wider class of non-smooth problems.

♻ ☆ Representing the Non-dominated Set of Multi-objective Network Problems by Supported Non-dominated Points

In multi-objective combinatorial optimization, unsupported non-dominated points typically outnumber supported points and are often significantly more challenging to compute. Recent studies show that extreme supported non-dominated points provide high-quality representations of the non-dominated set for certain binary problems. We demonstrate that this observation does not generalize to capacitated network optimization problems: representation quality decreases with increasing arc capacities, whereas supported non-dominated points consistently provide high-quality representations with respect to several quality indicators. However, supported point sets may still be too large in practical applications, where only a small, fixed number of alternatives is typically desired. Selecting fixed-size representations from the non-dominated set requires its computationally expensive generation and thus diminishes the computational advantages that representations are intended to provide. We therefore suggest the (extreme) supported points as alternative candidate sets in subset selection problems. Our numerical results show that restricting the candidate set to supported non-dominated points yields fixed-size representations of nearly the same quality as those selected from the complete non-dominated set. Overall, supported non-dominated points serve both as high-quality representations and as reasonable candidate sets for subset selection.
♻ ☆ A stochastic gradient algorithm for non-separable optimization with convergence guarantee

We study smooth parameterized non-separable objectives of the form $\mathcal L(θ)=F(Y(θ))$, where a global operator couples the outputs of all training samples. We analyze two stochastic gradient constructions within this output-space framework: the ideal per-batch gradient $G$, obtained by row sampling of the full output gradient, and a cached surrogate $H$ for parameterized updates in which full-data quantities are expensive to evaluate. For uniformly sampled batches, the ideal estimator has a deterministic batch-size scaling and a second moment controlled by the full output gradient. Using this structure, we establish local high-probability confinement and convergence for fixed positive step sizes on a prescribed parameter neighborhood under a power-type gradient inequality, with linear and polynomial regimes determined by its exponent. For the cached surrogate, a Lyapunov function couples the objective gap with the cache error and yields analogous local results on the corresponding non-exit event. The theory includes explicit path-length, confinement, and rate bounds; numerical experiments illustrate finite-budget decay trends and the effects of global output-gradient sampling, batch restriction, and cache tracking.

This paper presents a Markov-chain-based method for the early-phase analysis and design of spare-management architectures for large-scale satellite constellations. To assess the long-run viability of such concepts of operations, satellite failure and replenishment processes are modeled as Markov chains and analyzed through their stationary solution. We reinvestigate an indirect spare strategy, modeled as a multi-echelon periodic-review reorder-point/order-quantity policy, in which spares are first delivered to parking orbits and then transferred to constellation planes. The stock levels in constellation and parking orbits are each modeled as independent Markov chains, and a fixed-point iteration yields a consistent joint stationary solution that describes the strategy's average behavior. This approach accurately captures the stochastic interplay within a multi-echelon model driven by orbital mechanics, avoiding the aggregation assumptions of prior works and remaining valid across a wider operating domain. Building on this fast, accurate analysis, we formulate an optimization problem and solve it via a genetic algorithm. Finally, we demonstrate the practical value of both the analysis method and the optimization framework in a real-world mega-constellation case study.

We address this difficulty using multilevel subspace correction methods whose subspaces decompose the constraint kernel. Numerical experiments illustrate the outer convergence regimes and demonstrate parameter-robust behavior of the inner solvers across different meshes.

Our objective is to determine feedback gains that render the closed-loop system (strictly) passive with respect to the external port while minimizing the standard LQR cost in the disturbance-free case. The resulting constrained optimization problem is intractable due to bilinear matrix inequalities. We analyze the set of passivating gains, showing it is unbounded, possibly nonconvex, path-connected, and contractible. We propose an indirect approach, in which the set of passivating feedback gains is inner-approximated by a compact, convex polytope. A projected gradient flow is employed to compute a gain within this polytope that minimizes the LQR cost. Numerical examples illustrate the effectiveness of the method.

We consider one of the most common reparameterization techniques, the square transformation. Assuming the original objective function is the sum of a smooth function and a polyhedral function, we study the variational properties of the objective function after reparameterization. In particular, we first study the minimal norm of the subdifferential of the reparameterized objective function. Second, we compute the second subderivative of the reparameterized objective function on a linear subspace, which allows us to fully characterize the subclass of stationary points of the reparameterized objective function that correspond to stationary points of the original objective function. Finally, utilizing the representation of the minimal norm of the subdifferential, we show that the Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz (KL) exponent of the reparameterized function can be deduced from that of the original function. Applications to concrete optimization models are discussed.

♻ ☆ Stationary Mean-Field singular control of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process

Motivated by continuous-time optimal inventory management, we study a class of stationary mean-field control problems with singular controls. The dynamics are modeled by a mean-reverting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, and the performance criterion is given by a quadratic long-time average expected cost functional. The mean-field dependence is through the stationary mean of the controlled process itself, which enters the ergodic cost functional. We relate optimal controls for the stationary mean-field control problem to equilibria of an associated stationary mean-field game. In particular, optimal controls induce equilibria of the associated game, while the converse holds true within the class of admissible controls satisfying an additional integrability requirement. Finally, we solve the stationary mean-field game explicitly, thereby obtaining an explicitly characterized optimal reflection policy for the stationary mean-field control problem within this restricted class.

♻ ☆ Inventory Control and Storage Design via an $L^{\infty}$-control approach
Madhu Dhiman, Veeraruna Kavitha, Nandyala Hemachandra
Inventory control traditionally focuses on pricing and production rates, while physical storage capacity is typically fixed at the initial design stage. This paper addresses this relatively unexplored aspect by formulating a non-standard optimal control problem. The objective combines the classical integral term, capturing inventory-related costs, with an L^\infty-term, representing the maximum inventory level over the planning horizon. We first establish a relationship between the optimal pricing and production-rate policies, reducing the problem's dimensionality. Building on our earlier framework, we establish the existence of an optimal relaxed control and obtain an ε-optimal pure control for the reduced problem through smooth approximation. Numerical solutions of the resulting approximate problem demonstrate a substantial reduction in required storage capacity, with a negligible loss in net revenue (less than 6%), after accounting for shortage, holding, and production costs. We also observe that increasing the weight of the L^\infty-component reduces fluctuations in the inventory trajectory. These findings are particularly relevant when future demand information is incomplete or unavailable. In such settings, dynamically adjusting pricing and production policies to keep inventory levels close to zero can substantially reduce storage requirements with only a negligible loss in net revenue. Our results highlight the potential of incorporating inventory-level considerations directly into operational decision-making, particularly when physical storage capacity can be designed flexibly.
♻ ☆ Convergence of optimizers implies eigenvalues filtering at equilibrium

Ample empirical evidence in deep neural network training suggests that a variety of optimizers tend to find nearly global optima. In this article, we adopt the reversed perspective that convergence to an arbitrary point is assumed rather than proven, focusing on the consequences of this assumption. From this viewpoint, in line with recent advances on the edge-of-stability phenomenon, we argue that different optimizers effectively act as eigenvalue filters determined by their hyperparameters. Specifically, the standard gradient descent method inherently avoids the sharpest minima, whereas Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) algorithms go even further by actively favoring wider basins. Inspired by these insights, we propose two novel algorithms that exhibit enhanced eigenvalue filtering, effectively promoting wider minima. Our theoretical analysis leverages a generalized Hadamard--Perron stable manifold theorem and applies to general semialgebraic $C^2$ functions, without requiring additional non-degeneracy conditions or global Lipschitz bound assumptions. We support our conclusions with numerical experiments on feed-forward neural networks.

♻ ☆ Adaptively Incorporating Directional Hints into Zeroth-Order Optimization

We study zeroth-order optimization of nonconvex functions with the aid of directional hints, which are cheap but potentially inaccurate approximations of the true gradient direction, given by linear subspaces at each iteration. To leverage these hints adaptively while maintaining robustness to their quality, we introduce Control-Variate Zeroth-Order Descent (CV-ZOD), a new framework that refines the classical zeroth-order gradient estimator with a control variate that can be set based on the directional hints. We first show that the oracle algorithm that optimally sets the reference vector and step size at each iteration achieves a convergence rate that interpolates between the first-order $O(1/T)$ rate and the zeroth-order $O(d/T)$ rate, depending on the quality of the hints along the trajectory. We then develop a practical variant of CV-ZOD that achieves the same oracle guarantee up to logarithmic factors, without any prior knowledge of the hint quality. We validate the method empirically on simulation-based scientific optimization tasks, demonstrating sustained progress on nonconvex landscapes where zeroth-order descent is slower and existing guided methods stall as guidance deteriorates.
♻ ☆ Learning from the past in an irreversible investment problem

We consider an irreversible investment problem under incomplete information, where the investor decides whether and when to make investments in a project. Upon investment, the investor acquires previously hidden information from the project's past (''learning from the past''), and so the learning rate of the problem is controlled by investing. We set up this original problem as a recursively defined stopping problem with a learning-from-the-past effect. We show that, under general conditions, at each recursion step there exists a one-sided stopping boundary. We proceed to present the optimal investment strategy as a sequence of semi-explicit stopping boundaries derived from the smooth fit conditions of the corresponding free-boundary problems. Feasibility of our approach is then demonstrated by solving example boundaries numerically and by performing sensitivity analysis with respect to different model parameters.

♻ ☆ Difference of Convex Programming in the Wasserstein Space with Applications to MMD Optimization NeurIPS 2026
Clément Bonet, Pierre-Cyril Aubin-Frankowski, Youssef Mroueh
Optimizing functionals over the space of probability measures is now ubiquitous in machine learning. A widely used approach is to perform the optimization directly over the Wasserstein space, but many objective functionals of practical interest are non-convex along Wasserstein geodesics, making the analysis of standard first-order methods challenging. In this work, we study a class of objectives over the Wasserstein space that admit a difference-of-convex (DC) decomposition and we lift the classical convex-concave procedure (CCCP) to this setting. Under smoothness and strong convexity assumptions on the convex components of the decomposition, we prove almost stationarity along the iterates of the resulting algorithm. Our main focus is on the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and the Energy Distance (ED) functionals, for which we develop explicit Wasserstein DC decompositions, and establish local convergence of the scheme under mild assumptions. Empirically, we show that well-chosen DC decompositions yield faster and more stable convergence than Wasserstein gradient descent on these MMD objectives.

♻ ☆ Finite convergence and minimizer extraction in moment relaxations with correlative sparsity
Giovanni Fantuzzi, Federico Fuentes
We identify a new sufficient condition for the finite convergence of moment relaxations of polynomial optimization problems with correlative sparsity. This condition, which follows from a solution to a correlatively sparse version of the classical truncated moment problem, requires that certain moment matrices admit a flat extension and that the variable cliques underpinning the relaxation satisfy a "running intersection" property. We also describe an algorithm that, when these conditions are met, extracts at least as many minimizers for the original polynomial optimization problem as the largest rank of the moment matrices in its relaxation. Our results, along with the necessity of the running intersection property, are illustrated with examples.

Jaike van Twiller, Yossiri Adulyasak, Erick Delage, Djordje Grbic, Rune Møller Jensen
Reinforcement learning (RL) has successfully solved various deterministic and stochastic planning problems. However, conventional RL struggles with complex real-world constraints, particularly when feasibility is explicit and depends on the current state or trajectory. In this work, we address stochastic sequential decision-making with state-dependent constraints through a real-world case study of the master stowage planning problem in container shipping, which aims to optimize revenue and costs under demand uncertainty and operational constraints. We propose a deep RL framework with an encoder-decoder model that integrates problem instance, solution, and uncertainty information to guide planning. We introduce differentiable projection layers that enforce convex polyhedral constraints, while Jacobian corrections offset the projections to yield unbiased policy gradient estimates. Experiments show that our model efficiently finds adaptive, feasible solutions that generalize across distribution shifts and scale to longer planning horizons, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in constrained RL and stochastic programming. As such, our policies enable adaptive, uncertainty-aware planning that can support resilient and sustainable supply chains.

♻ ☆ Robust Parallel Machine Scheduling: A Comparison of Robustness Measures and Local Search Approaches
Casper Loman, Loriana Pascual, Bram Elderhorst, Marjan van den Akker, Roel van den Broek, Han Hoogeveen
In many real-world scheduling problems, the processing times of tasks are subject to uncertainty. This makes it essential to design schedules that are robust against disruptions. We distinguish between two types of robustness: quality-robust schedules keep a stable objective value under disruptions, while solution-robust schedules keep a stable schedule structure. We study how to generate schedules for the Stochastic Parallel Machine Scheduling Problem (SPMSP) with precedence constraints and release dates that are both quality- and solution-robust. To this end, we compare several robustness measures and local search algorithms that use these measures. We start with an extensive simulation study where we determine the correlation of 13 existing and 6 new robustness measures with both quality and solution robustness. Next, we use the measures with high robustness correlation as the objective in our local search algorithm to find the best way to generate schedules containing both job-machine assignments as well as buffer assignments. We use a new dynamic objective weight within our local search algorithms, which actively changes the objective weights in each iteration. We found that the best way to generate robust schedules is to use robustness measures that model the processing times with normal distribution approximations and to combine job placement and buffer assignment simultaneously.

Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed-loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier-drift condition is formulated as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite-horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime-validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/runtime-barrier-monitor.

♻ ☆ The complexity landscape of robust (integer) linear programming
Michael Poss, Jannis Kurtz, Marc Goerigk, Dorothee Henke
We study the computational complexity of the decision versions of three classic classes of robust optimization problems: static robust optimization, two-stage (adjustable) robust optimization, and $K$-adaptability. We consider that the feasibility sets, the uncertainty sets, and the recourse sets are polyhedra or integer-programming-representable sets, the uncertainty is decision-independent or decision-dependent, and the feasible regions are bounded or unbounded. While these problems are well-established in the current literature, we give a systematic classification that places them in the complexity classes $\mathsf{P}$, $\mathsf{NP}$, $\mathsf{coNP}$, and higher levels of the polynomial hierarchy ($Σ_2^p$ and $Σ_3^p$), and, once decision-dependent uncertainty introduces quadratic constraints, in the existential theory of the reals and its hierarchy ($\exists\mathbb{R}$, $Σ_2\mathbb{R}$, and $Σ_3\mathbb{R}$) or among the undecidable problems. Beyond hardness reductions, we pay particular attention to membership proofs, establishing polynomial-size certificates even though the sets considered generally contain vectors of exponential encoding length. As a by-product, we give an alternative proof that bilevel linear optimization lies in $\mathsf{NP}$, exploiting its connection to decision-dependent robust optimization. For $K$-adaptability, we relate the problem to its static and two-stage counterparts, showing that hardness grows monotonically with $K$ and that, for fully discrete decision-dependent instances, $K$-adaptability reduces back to the static problem.

By design these minimizers are Hölder curves or Hölder parametrizations of surfaces whose images generally have a non-integer Hausdorff dimension. Their origin is deterministic, but their regularity properties are roughly similar to those of typical realizations of stochastic processes. As a key tool and our main technical result, we prove novel continuity and boundedness results for potentials of occupation measures of Gaussian random fields. These results complement well-known results for local times, but hold under much less restrictive assumptions. In an auxiliary section, we generalize earlier results on nonlinear compositions of fractional Sobolev functions with $BV$-functions to higher dimensions.

In such settings, derivatives may be difficult to obtain, and evaluating different control actions through repeated trajectory simulations can be expensive. We propose Hamiltonian Primal-Dual Policy Optimization (HPDPO), a method that uses numerical costates to guide the search for improved controls. The costates are estimated using finite differences of the numerical model and are used to rank candidate actions. Rather than performing a full remaining-horizon simulation for every candidate, HPDPO evaluates a small set of promising alternatives and accepts a control update only when it decreases the discrete objective. We derive a first-order costate-based approximation for ranking candidate actions and establish descent of the discretized objective under rollout-verified updates. We test the method on scalar and multidimensional control problems, including examples with nonsmooth and learned dynamics. The results show good agreement with analytical or published reference solutions and lower simulation costs than the direct-rollout methods considered. HPDPO requires only forward model evaluations, without analytical or automatically differentiated derivatives of the dynamics or a learned value function.

The algorithm combines a retrospective-approximation strategy for handling the objective and an interior-point approach for handling the constraints. In each iteration of an outer loop, the objective is approximated by an empirical average over a set of realizations of the random variable argument and the resulting sampled problem is solved with an interior-point method that allows inexact search-direction computations for computational flexibility. Termination conditions for the interior-point method are tailored for those needed for convergence guarantees by the outer loop. Over the outer loop, the sample set is updated adaptively in such a manner that convergence guarantees for solving the original optimization problem can be assured. The results of numerical experiments are presented, which show that the proposed algorithm can outperform competing methods that have comparable theoretical guarantees.

The dynamic formulation of optimal transport, also known as the Benamou-Brenier formulation, has been extended to the unbalanced case by introducing a source term in the continuity equation. ♻ ☆ Overcoming Demand Censoring through Randomization for Risk-Sensitive Newsvendor Learning
Zhengchao Wang, Nam Ho-Nguyen
We study online newsvendor learning with bounded demand, censored observations, and convex nonlinear shortage costs. Because stockouts can conceal the shortage magnitudes needed by gradient-based algorithms, we use randomized ordering to construct unbiased subgradient estimates. We characterize admissible randomization distributions within this framework and develop an online inventory policy that combines the resulting subgradient estimates with gradient-based updates. Our regret analysis quantifies the cost of randomization via the estimation variance and an additional loss term. We characterize the randomization distributions that minimize this objective. For piecewise-linear shortage costs, the optimal distribution is computed through a linear-time recursion; for costs with bounded curvature density, it is characterized by a scalar ordinary differential equation. The policy achieves expected regret of $O(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed order in hindsight over $T$ periods. Under independent demand and suitable curvature of expected losses, the bound improves to $O(\sqrt{T})$. Matching minimax lower bounds establish rate optimality over the corresponding classes with a fixed marginal-cost bound. Both rates extend to nonperishable inventory under uniformly positive conditional expected demand. Numerical experiments on synthetic and retail data show improvements over alternative policies using censored observations.

♻ ☆ Parallel Newton methods for the continuous quadratic knapsack problem: A Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel tale
Leonardo D. Secchin, Paulo J. S. Silva
The continuous quadratic knapsack (CQK) problem involves minimizing a diagonal convex quadratic function subject to box constraints and a single linear equality constraint. It has numerous applications in resource allocation, multicommodity flow, machine learning, and classical optimization tasks such as Lagrangian relaxation and quasi-Newton updates. In this work, we revisit the semismooth Newton method introduced by Cominetti, Mascarenhas, and Silva. We demonstrate that the method can be significantly improved in two directions. First, for projections onto the simplex or the $\ell_1$-ball, it can incorporate Condat's highly effective initial multiplier guess. Second, it can serve as a flexible foundation for CQK algorithms, allowing for different parallel variants tailored to exploit CPU and GPU computational models. These improvements are implemented in the open-source Julia package \texttt{NewtonCQK.jl}. We present extensive numerical tests comparing this implementation with other state-of-the-art solvers, demonstrating its superior efficiency and scalability.
♻ ☆ Continuous-time mean field games: a primal-dual characterization
Xin Guo, Anran Hu, Jiacheng Zhang, Yufei Zhang
This paper establishes a primal-dual formulation for continuous-time mean field games (MFGs) and provides a complete analytical characterization of the set of all mean field equilibria (MFEs). We reformulate the representative player's control problem as a linear program over occupation measures and derive its dual formulation over smooth subsolutions of the associated Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation. This primal-dual formulation yields a verification theorem for MFEs under measurable coefficients and provides necessary and sufficient conditions characterizing all MFEs under a strong duality condition. We establish this strong duality for nondegenerate diffusions with Hölder continuous coefficients through a new global $C^{2,α}$ regularity result for fully nonlinear parabolic HJB equations. A key insight is that the dual variable need only coincide with the HJB solution on the support of the mean field flow. Compared with existing approaches, our characterization requires neither convexity of the Hamiltonian nor uniqueness of its optimizer, accommodates relaxed equilibria, and remains applicable when the HJB equation lacks classical solutions.

☆ Resolvent Ellipsoid for Minty Set Inclusions NeurIPS
Ashkan Soleymani, Gabriele Farina, Patrick Jaillet
We study Minty set inclusion on a compact convex set $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ with a set-valued operator $A : \mathcal{X} \rightrightarrows \mathbb{R}^d$. Under the Minty promise, the goal is to compute $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $u \in A(x)$ such that $\sup_{y \in \mathcal{X}} \langle u, x - y \rangle \le \varepsilon$. Our approach is geometric and we work in the fixed-scale constrained-resolvent oracle model, where a query at anchor $a$ is assumed to return a resolvent point $x^+$ together with the Yosida vector $g_η(a) = (a - x^+)/η$. We prove that each oracle response yields a sharp dichotomy: either the returned point provides an $\varepsilon$-SVI certificate, or the Yosida vector defines a strict separating normal for the Minty set. Thus, a single black-box resolvent query supplies either a certified candidate solution or a valid geometric cut. Combining this separation principle with the ellipsoid method, we obtain RESOLVENT-ELLIPSOID, an algorithm that computes an $\varepsilon$-SVI in $\mathcal{O}\!\left(\operatorname{poly}(d, \log(1/\varepsilon))\right)$ black-box oracle calls to the fixed-scale constrained resolvent. For monotone inclusions, our algorithm gives, to our knowledge, the first $\mathcal{O}\!\left(\mathrm{poly}(d, \log(1/\varepsilon))\right)$ black-box guarantee in the fixed-scale resolvent model.

☆ The Canonical Family of Reduced Row Pivot Echelon Forms and the Induced Lexicographic Canonical Algorithm for Linear Programming
A. G. Paraskevopoulos, D. A. Patsouras
A complete canonical family of uniquely normalized, row-equivalent representatives of an $m\times n$ matrix is introduced and termed the family of Reduced Row Pivot Echelon Forms (RRPEFs). All RRPEFs represent the same row space, with the standard reduced row echelon form, renamed the Upper RREF (URREF), and the Lower RREF (LRREF) as its extreme members. A reformulation of Noether's Complementary Subspace Basis Theorem yields normalized bases of the row space that coincide with the nonzero rows of the corresponding RRPEFs. Constructively, each RRPEF is obtained by multi-index Gauss--Jordan reduction of a nonsingular transition submatrix. Factoring the admissible pivot-index sets by equality of their associated RRPEFs yields a quotient set in canonical bijection with the set of distinct RRPEFs. This bijection transfers the strict lexicographic order to the distinct RRPEFs and induces a finite chain from the URREF to the LRREF. The resulting structure gives rise to the Induced Lexicographic Canonical Algorithm (ILCA). Lexicographic confinement and singular-transition skipping restrict the candidate domain, whereas RRPEF reuse and scalar-equivalent transition bypassing avoid redundant Gauss--Jordan reductions while retaining the corresponding basic-solution tableaux. Strict lexicographic progression prevents cycling, while the traversal proceeds independently of objective improvement under degeneracy-induced stalling. ILCA terminates when a feasible tableau satisfies the standard optimality conditions and otherwise completes the finite traversal, including for Tucker- and Cunningham-type totally degenerate configurations.

☆ Receding horizon control with sensor-induced positive semidefinite state penalization
Behzad Azmi, Sergio S. Rodrigues
This paper develops and analyzes a receding horizon control (RHC) framework for the stabilization of infinite-dimensional nonautonomous continuous-time systems with an infinite-horizon control objective. The considered stage costs penalize only a finite-dimensional component of the state and are therefore positive semidefinite with respect to the full state. Without imposing terminal costs or terminal constraints, we establish exponential stability and derive suboptimality estimates under suitable stabilizability and detectability-type assumptions, together with an online selection of the sampling times. In the linear case, we extend the framework to output-feedback RHC by combining it with a Luenberger-type state estimator based on finitely many sensors, and establish closed-loop stability using an augmented Lyapunov functional. The abstract state-feedback results are verified for a nonlinear Schlögl parabolic equation around an unstable steady state and, in the output-feedback setting, for nonautonomous linear parabolic equations. The control and observation realizations involve finite-dimensional actuation and sensing, including localized boundary controls and spatially localized state-penalization operators. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and illustrate the performance of the proposed RHC schemes.
♻ ☆ Conditions for Normality of Pontryagin's Maximum Principle in the Absence of State Constraints
André Tits, Pierre-Antoine Absil, Noé Tits
Pontryagin's Maximum Principle is said to be "normal" for the problem at hand when it has a solution (maximizer u*) that explicitly involves the problem's cost function, making the maximum principle helpful (while in the opposite situation it is of no help). The aim of the present paper is, for Lagrange optimal control problems without state constraints, to identify classes of problems for which the Principle is normal. General conditions are introduced that guarantee normality, and classes of problems that satisfy these conditions are identified. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the control values) "augmented" reachable set, with cost along an upward vertical axis, has a convex lower-boundary function and the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the reachable state set, with the terminal constraint within the affine hull of that set. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the values of the control signal) "augmented" (with the cost value along an upward "vertical axis") reachable set has a "convex" lower boundary for which the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the set of reachable states. Special attention is given to Lagrange steering problems: sufficient conditions are obtained on a nested sequence of sub-classes of such problems, culminating with the class of steering problems with scalar control signal and linear time-invariant (LTI) state dynamics and objective integrand, for which normality is guaranteed whenever all eigenvalues of the state dynamics matrix A are real (e.g., if A is symmetric or triangular or the system is overdamped) or have small enough imaginary parts; simple 2 x 2 examples show that, in contrast with the situation in the finite-dimensional case, this property does not extend to arbitrary A matrices.
♻ ☆ Competition Versus Complexity in Multiple-Selection Prophet Inequalities
Eugenio Cruz-Ossa, Sebastian Perez-Salazar, Victor Verdugo
Competition complexity formalizes a compelling intuition: rather than refining the mechanism, how much additional competition is sufficient for a simple mechanism to compete with an optimal one? We begin the study of this question in multi-unit pricing for welfare maximization using prophet inequalities. An online decision-maker observes $m \geq k$ nonnegative values drawn independently from a known distribution, may select up to $k$ of them, and aims to maximize the expected sum of selected values. The benchmark is a prophet who observes a sequence of length $n \geq k$ and selects the $k$ largest values. We focus on the widely adopted class of single-threshold algorithms and fully characterize their $(1-\varepsilon)$-competition complexity. Notably, our results reveal a sharp competition-induced phase transition: in the absence of competition, single-threshold algorithms are fundamentally limited to a $1-1/\sqrt{2kπ}$ fraction of the prophet value, whereas even a $1\%$ multiplicative increase beyond $n$ observations suffices to achieve a $1-\exp(-Θ(k))$ fraction. Another notable result happens when $k=1$: we show that the $(1-\varepsilon)$-competition complexity is exactly $\ln(1/\varepsilon)$, fully resolving an open question by Brustle et al. [Math. Oper. Res. 2024]. Our analysis is based on infinite-dimensional linear programming and duality arguments.
